text: ## What is Osteoarthritis? Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis among older people and affects roughly one-third of adults aged 65+. The condition develops when cartilage — the cushioning tissue at bone ends — deteriorates, potentially allowing bones to contact each other directly. This primarily impacts hands, knees, hips, spine, neck, and lower back, though it affects just joints, not internal organs. ## What Causes Osteoarthritis? The disease stems from years of wear and tear on joints affecting cartilage structure. Contributing factors include advancing age, repetitive joint stress from prior injuries, misaligned joints, and excess body weight. Research suggests osteoarthritis results from a combination of factors in the body and the environment. ## What Are the Symptoms? Common warning indicators include joint pain, swelling or tenderness in one or more joints, stiffness following rest periods, and a crunching feeling or sound of bone rubbing on bone.

text: ## What Are the Symptoms? Common warning indicators include joint pain, swelling or tenderness in one or more joints, stiffness following rest periods, and a crunching feeling or sound of bone rubbing on bone. Notably, only approximately one-third of individuals with X-ray evidence of osteoarthritis actually experience noticeable symptoms. ## What Are the Treatments? Management strategies encompass exercise (strengthening, aerobic, range-of-motion activities), weight control, heat/cold therapy, and surgical interventions when necessary. Options include arthroscopic debridement, bone repositioning, or joint replacement. Current treatments can relieve symptoms such as pain and disability, but right now there are no treatments that can cure osteoarthritis.

text: ## What is (are) Bursitis? A bursa is a small, fluid-filled sac that acts as a cushion between a bone and other moving parts, such as muscles, tendons, or skin. Bursitis occurs when a bursa becomes inflamed. People get bursitis by overusing a joint. It can also be caused by an injury. It usually occurs at the knee or elbow. Kneeling or leaning your elbows on a hard surface for a long time can make bursitis start. Doing the same kinds of movements every day or putting stress on joints increases your risk. Symptoms of bursitis include pain and swelling. Your doctor will diagnose bursitis with a physical exam and tests such as x-rays and MRIs. He or she may also take fluid from the swollen area to be sure the problem isn't an infection. Treatment of bursitis includes rest or ice.

text: ## What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when the median nerve, which runs from the forearm into the palm of the hand, becomes pressed or squeezed at the wrist. The condition involves a narrow passageway containing both nerve and tendons. Thickening from irritated tendons or other swelling narrows this tunnel, compressing the nerve. Symptoms typically develop gradually, beginning with numbness and tingling in the hand and wrist. As the condition progresses, grasping objects becomes increasingly difficult. Women experience carpal tunnel syndrome three times more frequently than men. Contributing factors include trauma or wrist injury, thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and pregnancy-related fluid retention. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent permanent nerve damage. ## What is the Outlook for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? The condition responds well to treatment, though outcomes vary.

Initial management typically involves immobilizing the wrist with a splint. For more severe cases, surgical intervention may be recommended when conservative approaches prove insufficient.

text: ## What is Back Pain? Back pain is one of the most prevalent medical conditions, affecting 8 out of 10 people at some point during their lives. The condition manifests as either acute (sudden onset lasting days to weeks) or chronic (persisting beyond three months). Symptoms can range from dull, constant aches to sharp, sudden pain and may result from trauma, sports injuries, or everyday activities. ## Treatments for Back Pain Management approaches focus on restoring function and preventing recurrence. Treatment options include: - Hot or cold compresses to reduce pain and inflammation - Limited bed rest (maximum 1-2 days; prolonged rest can worsen symptoms) - Exercise to strengthen back and abdominal muscles - Physical therapy - In severe cases, surgical intervention The goal is to restore proper function and strength to the back, and prevent recurrence of the injury. ## Outlook for Back Pain Most patients recover favorably.

text: ## What is Intervertebral Disc Disease? Intervertebral disc disease (IDD) is a common musculoskeletal condition that primarily affects the back. It is characterized by intervertebral disc herniation and/or sciatic pain (sciatica) and is a primary cause of low back pain, affecting about 5% of individuals. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute to its development. Treatment options range from conservative approaches like physical therapy to surgical interventions when necessary. ## What Causes Intervertebral Disc Disease? IDD results from multiple interacting factors. Factors such as occupational stress, trauma, or obesity, together with genetic alterations, may result in the structural weakness of a disc, cause a herniation, and possibly initiate a cascade of events leading to sciatica and pathological disc changes. One of the best-known environmental risk factors for IDD is vibration in occupational driving. Inflammation also plays a significant role in disease progression. ## What Are the Treatments for Intervertebral Disc Disease?

In the absence of red flags, the initial approach to treatment is typically conservative and includes physical therapy. Most acute cases resolve favorably: in 90% of affected individuals, acute attacks of sciatica usually improve within 4 to 6 weeks without surgical intervention. When necessary, surgical options include discectomy or spinal fusion procedures.

text: ## What is Gout? Gout is a common, painful form of arthritis. It causes swollen, red, hot and stiff joints. The condition develops when uric acid builds up in the body, forming needle-like crystals in joints. It typically first attacks the big toe but can affect ankles, heels, knees, wrists, fingers, and elbows. Early attacks usually improve within days, though over time they become longer and more frequent. ## Who is at Risk? Risk factors include: - Genetics: many people with gout have a family history of the disease - Demographics: more common in men than women; more common in adults than children - Weight: being overweight increases risk due to excess uric acid production - Alcohol: drinking too much alcohol can lead to a buildup of uric acid because alcohol interferes with the removal of uric acid from the body - Diet: high-purine foods like liver, dried beans, peas, and anchovies

text: ## What is (are) Herniated Disk? The spine consists of 26 vertebrae with soft disks between them that provide cushioning. As people age, these disks degenerate and lose their cushioning ability, potentially causing pain. A herniated disk occurs when the disk ruptures, allowing the jelly-like center of the disk to leak, irritating the nearby nerves. This can result in sciatica or back pain. Diagnosis involves a physical exam and sometimes imaging tests. Treatment options include rest, physical therapy, and sometimes surgery. Most people recover with appropriate treatment. NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: ## What is (are) Spinal Stenosis? Your spine, or backbone, protects your spinal cord and allows you to stand and bend. Spinal stenosis causes narrowing in your spine. The narrowing puts pressure on your nerves and spinal cord and can cause pain. Spinal stenosis occurs mostly in people older than 50. Younger people with a spine injury or a narrow spinal canal are also at risk. Diseases such as arthritis and scoliosis can cause spinal stenosis, too. Symptoms might appear gradually or not at all. They include: - Pain in your neck or back - Numbness, weakness, cramping, or pain in your arms or legs - Pain going down the leg - Foot problems Doctors diagnose spinal stenosis with a physical exam and imaging tests. Treatments include physical therapy, braces, and surgery. NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: ## What is (are) Sprains and Strains? A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. Ligaments are tissues that connect bones at a joint. Falling, twisting, or getting hit can all cause a sprain. Ankle and wrist sprains are common. Symptoms include pain, swelling, bruising, and being unable to move your joint. You might feel a pop or tear when the injury happens. A strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon. Tendons are tissues that connect muscle to bone. Twisting or pulling these tissues can cause a strain. Strains can happen suddenly or develop over time. Back and hamstring muscle strains are common. Many people get strains playing sports. Symptoms include pain, muscle spasms, swelling, and trouble moving the muscle. At first, treatment of both sprains and strains usually involves resting the injured area, icing it, and wearing a bandage or device that compresses the area.
